entry.title: Sam Gilliam：變化、抽象藝術與自由
entry.content:
今天我去參觀了 Sam Gilliam 的展覽。展覽主要圍繞 Sam Gilliam 如何讓抽象藝術延伸到畫框之外進行布展。展廳內的主體是 Gilliam 的懸垂繪畫（Drape Paintings），這些作品將畫布懸掛在牆上或天花板上，邀請參觀者和展廳環境參與到作品呈現之中。有趣的是，展廳裡還有許多現代設計的椅子，地面上放置了一些大型坐墊，鼓勵觀眾坐下，甚至躺下來，從不同角度觀察這些三維的藝術作品。

Sam Gilliam 其人

Sam Gilliam 出生於密西西比州圖珀洛（Tupelo），成長於肯塔基州路易維爾（Louisville），1962 年遷居華盛頓特區，並在那裡度過了絕大部分藝術生涯。

Gilliam 最著名的是他的懸垂繪畫（Drape Paintings），這些作品將畫布懸掛在牆上或天花板上，創造出一種動態的、三維的視覺效果。他的作品打破了傳統繪畫的界限，使觀眾能夠從不同角度欣賞藝術品。

這種繪畫打破了傳統的二維畫布概念，同時邀請觀眾參與到畫中，從不同角度觀察作品。畫與展覽的空間環境互動，重力、光線、空氣流動等因素參與到作品的呈現中。觀眾的感知也會隨著觀看時間產生變化。作品並不會在第一眼就完全呈現。不同的層次、色彩關係和視覺節奏，需要通過持續觀看逐漸被發現。作品是一直動態變化的，永恆不止，沒有完成的狀態。觀眾的參與和感知成為作品的一部分，形成了獨特的藝術體驗。

變奏

即興並不取代結構，而是依賴結構。

Gilliam 很喜歡爵士樂。他在創作作品的時候，常常會一邊聽著爵士樂的旋律，一邊讓自己的藝術思維在畫紙上展開。爵士音樂家通常從共同的旋律、節奏或和絃變化出發，在這個基礎上進行變奏。一段音樂可以重複、偏離、拆解，然後重新組合。Gilliam 也以類似的方法進行創作。他不斷回到此前探索過的觀念，卻通過材料、尺度和製作過程的變化，使舊觀念產生新形式。

爵士樂也成為他藝術生活的一部分。他的創作不是以一個固定終點開始，而是從調整、發現出發，再不斷推進。

Gilliam 的藝術通過重複、變奏、偶然性和持續探索，在形式與結構之間創造自由。

何為藝術

這件藝術作品想表達什麼？僅僅是形式嗎？還是什麼？我在欣賞這些繪畫的時候，是看不出來具體的內容的，只有色彩、線條、層次、材料。

藝術的意義在於什麼？

長久以來，人們試圖通過藝術再現世界、表達情感、傳遞思想。一幅畫可以描繪山川河流、人物肖像，一首詩可以記錄某種心境，一部小說可以講述一段人生。我們習慣於追問一件藝術作品所表達的內容，試圖在畫面、文字和聲音背後尋找某種可以被理解和言說的意義。

然而，藝術的價值是否必須依附於它所表現的對象？假如一幅畫不再描繪任何具體事物，只剩下色彩、線條與形狀；假如一首詩沒有完整的敘事，只剩下語言的節奏、重複與斷裂，它們是否仍然可以被稱為藝術？

在 Sam Gilliam 的抽象繪畫面前，這個問題變得格外具體。色彩相互滲透，顏料留下不規則的痕跡，畫布摺疊、懸垂，在空間中形成複雜的層次。我們很難從中辨認出明確的對象，也未必能夠概括出一個確定的主題。然而，這並不妨礙我們感受到變化、運動、張力與節奏。作品的意義似乎不再隱藏於形式背後，而是直接產生於形式本身。

藝術不只是關於內容，也關於形式。而形式並非僅僅是傳遞內容的工具。顏色之間的關係、語言的節奏、音樂的停頓，甚至材料自身的質地，都可以創造無法被其他表達方式完全替代的經驗。

藝術的意義在於沒有意義？或者說，都是意義？

追求自由

懸垂繪畫體現了一種挑戰傳統、突破二維侷限性的自由。色彩和材料從畫框中解放出來，在空間中自然流動。觀眾從固定的觀察位置中解放出來，可以從不同角度、不同距離去感受作品。

1960 年代的美國，正處於一個充滿變革與動盪的時代。民權運動、反越戰運動以及一系列社會文化思潮，衝擊著既有的社會秩序。1968 年，馬丁·路德·金遇刺，抗議與騷亂席捲美國多個城市。與此同時，社會對於平等、身份與自由的討論也愈發激烈。

Sam Gilliam 正是在這樣的時代背景下開展他的藝術實驗。作為一名非裔美國藝術家，他不僅經歷了種族隔離與民權運動，也面對著藝術創作中的身份問題。當時，一些人期待黑人藝術家通過具象作品直接呈現種族歧視、社會抗爭與黑人群體的歷史經驗。然而，Gilliam 堅持抽象繪畫，拒絕讓自己的藝術被某一種身份或表達方式所限定。

這並不意味著他對社會現實漠不關心。他的作品《April 4》便以馬丁·路德·金遇刺的日期命名。歷史事件可以進入他的繪畫，卻不一定要以人物、場景或明確的政治符號出現。藝術的政治性，也不必完全依賴於它所描繪的內容。

在這一意義上，Gilliam 對抽象藝術的堅持，本身便可以被理解為一種自由的實踐：藝術家有權選擇如何表達，也有權拒絕外界為自己的創作預先規定主題與形式。

作為藝術的文學

從繪畫回到文學，我們似乎也習慣於追問一首詩表達了怎樣的情感，一部小說講述了怎樣的故事，而較少注意語言本身。事實上，文字並非透明的媒介。詞語的排列、句子的長短、敘述的節奏、意象的重複與變奏，都參與著文學意義的生成。正如 Sam Gilliam 將色彩與畫布從既定的形式中解放出來，文學也可以不再完全服從線性的敘事與預設的主題。爵士樂式的即興、不同時間與記憶的交疊、語言在重複中發生的微妙變化，都可以成為文學創造的方式。作家未必需要在動筆之前就知道作品最終要去往何處；有時候，恰恰是在文字的展開之中，我們才發現那些尚未形成的思想。文學因此不只是記錄生活、表達思想的工具，也是一種探索未知的藝術。我們通過語言認識世界，也在創造語言的過程中，重新發現世界。

entry.title: 沒有隨身碟的 Arch 安裝記
entry.content:
初中的時候有一種自由探索的快樂，當時用了一段時間 Arch Linux，可以什麼都不想，沉浸在這種技術之中，進入程式設計的心流，沒有 AI 打擾，沒有效率至上，沒有功利主義。程式設計是一種禪修。現在一切都變了，程式設計變成了工作，無休止的 agent 工作。再也回不來了？

於是我突然非常想給我的 Windows PC 安裝上 Arch Linux 雙系統，正好我最近的研究任務也需要一個 Linux 環境。

手邊沒有隨身碟，於是打算直接從硬碟啟動安裝映像。具體思路是，建立一個臨時分割區作為安裝媒體，之後可以改作 swap 分割區。

從 Windows 分出約 150 GB，140 GB 留給 Arch，另外 10 GB 暫時充當安裝媒體。

直到 Windows 在重新啟動後，留給我一行 INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE。

有點諷刺，最開始，我都在使用 ChatGPT，讓它判斷狀態，再照著建議繼續操作。從壓縮磁碟區、設定 ISO 啟動，到 GPT 分割區和 GRUB，它總能接著給出下一步。解釋連貫，指令具體，於是我也逐漸省去了自己的核對。最後把 Windows 搞壞了。

後來回看，問題恰好藏在這個「下一步」裡：它未必正確理解了眼前的機器，卻仍然可以繼續回答。

這篇記下當時的分割區、啟動過程，以及最後留下的問題。指令是操作記錄，並非一份可以照抄的安裝教學。到整理這篇文章時，Arch 已經能啟動，Windows 的恢復仍未完成。

先從一塊磁碟開始

電腦是 HP Victus Gaming，使用 Samsung NVMe SSD。原有的 Windows 11 裝在啟用 BitLocker 的 C 槽，採用 UEFI 啟動，Secure Boot 最初也是開啟的。安裝媒體和兩個系統，都要放在這同一塊 SSD 上。

第一個障礙出現在 Windows 的磁碟管理。C 槽明明還有很多可用空間，能壓縮出來的容量卻很少。查看系統事件記錄中的 Event ID 259，才發現限制壓縮的不可移動檔案，包括 pagefile.sys 和 NTFS 的 $Extend\$UsnJrnl。微軟的磁碟區壓縮文件也提到不可移動檔案造成的限制，以及透過事件記錄定位檔案的方法。其中一條記錄是：

關閉分頁檔等操作之後，可壓縮空間有所增加，最後取得了約 150 GB。後來用 PowerShell 重新列出分割區：

當時的對應關係如下。這裡按編號列出，並不代表它們在磁碟上的實際排列順序。

分割區磁碟代號容量用途
p1—512 MiBEFI System Partition
p2—16 MiBMicrosoft Reserved
p3C:325.46 GiBWindows，BitLocker 加密
p4—約 985 MiBWindows Recovery
p5D:140 GiB預留給 Arch
p6E:10 GiBArch 安裝媒體

這張表後來成了整次排查中最需要反覆確認的東西。ChatGPT 曾把 p4、p5、p6 的用途對錯，混淆了 Windows Recovery、Arch 的預留空間和安裝媒體，卻仍然給出針對具體分割區的操作建議。

p5 只是一個編號。真正需要確認的是它的大小、類型、位置，以及裡面裝著什麼。這些資訊不能靠對話中的印象補齊。

C 槽當時的 BitLocker 狀態也值得留下：

系統當下能讀取 C 槽，不代表它沒有加密。後續又會修改 EFI 和啟動設定，恢復金鑰是否可用、出了問題要從哪裡回去，本來就應該在動手前確認。微軟的 BitLocker 復原概觀列出了啟動管理員、分割區表或 TPM 等變更可能觸發復原的情況。

安裝變成了搶修

我把 Arch ISO 裡的檔案複製到 E:，將這個 FAT32 分割區的卷標設為 ARCH-OS，再檢查 Live 環境需要的檔案是否存在：

原來的啟動設定使用 archisosearchuuid 尋找 ISO 檔案系統。現在檔案被複製到一般的 FAT32 分割區，尋找安裝媒體的方式也要跟著改。

這裡其實隔著兩個步驟：UEFI 先找到 EFI 程式並執行；接著，Linux 的 initramfs 還要找到 Arch Live 的檔案系統。前一步成功，並不保證後一步也成功。當時很多看似相近的「啟動問題」，都需要這樣拆開才說得清楚。

在後續的分割區和啟動設定調整之後，Windows 無法啟動了。

從這時開始，原本的安裝變成了搶修。我重新進入 HP BIOS。

啟動項裡顯然沒有剛剛做好的那個 Arch 安裝媒體。

我最開始試圖透過 PXE 啟動 Arch。我從來沒有玩過 PXE，但是這台機器不支援 iPXE，也不知道該怎麼透過網路啟動 Arch。

後來我自己找了半天，發現這台機器支援 Boot From EFI File。我便直接從硬碟上的 Arch 安裝媒體進入 Live 環境。沒有 Windows 恢復隨身碟，這個原本用來安裝新系統的環境，暫時成了檢查舊系統的入口。

先看磁碟和分割區表：

GPT、EFI、BitLocker 系統分割區和 Recovery 都是排查的重點。不過，「分割區還在」只能回答很有限的問題，並不能據此認定 Windows 還能正常啟動。BitLocker 加密的分割區也不能直接當作一般 NTFS 磁碟區，拿 ntfsfix 試著修一遍。

當時沒有查明唯一根因。INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE（0x7B）表示 Windows 在啟動過程中無法存取系統分割區；儲存控制器模式、驅動、檔案系統和啟動設定，都可能需要檢查。僅憑這行錯誤，還不能把問題歸結為 EFI 檔案損壞。

同樣，故障發生在那些操作之後，也不足以證明某一條指令就是唯一原因。但分割區映射被理解錯誤、接著仍有具體的修改建議，這件事是明確的。它讓原本就不簡單的排查，又多了一層不確定。

我先按照 ArchWiki 的安裝指南安裝。安裝過程其實很熟悉，有些指令都能背出來了。過去這麼多年。

能啟動的 GRUB，留不住的啟動項

Arch 裝好後，接著設定 GRUB。第一次安裝就遇到：

這一次是把 /boot 和 EFI System Partition 混在了一起。/boot 可以只是 Linux 根檔案系統中的一個目錄；grub-install 的 --efi-directory 則需要指向已掛載的 EFI 系統分割區。這個參數的用法，可以對照 ArchWiki 的 GRUB 安裝說明。

原有的 EFI 分割區是 FAT32 格式的 p1。將它掛載到 /efi 之後，安裝方式是：

EFI 分割區中也出現了相應的檔案：

然而重新啟動後，HP 韌體仍然選擇 Windows 的啟動路徑。用 efibootmgr -v 檢查，找不到能持續保留的 Arch 啟動項；嘗試建立 UEFI NVRAM 項目，重啟後又消失了。BIOS 中也沒有可用的 Customized Boot 選項。

有一條路卻是通的：從 HP 的 Boot From EFI File 手動選擇 EFI/GRUB/grubx64.efi，便能進入 GRUB。

至少可以確定，這份 GRUB EFI 檔案能被韌體載入。接下來需要處理的，是韌體究竟選擇哪條路徑，以及為什麼自訂啟動項無法保留。

最後採用了一個繞行的辦法。既然手動選擇 grubx64.efi 已經能進入 GRUB，而新建立的啟動項又留不住，我便不再依靠新增的 Arch 啟動項，轉而使用這台機器仍會自動選擇的 Windows Boot Manager 路徑。

在這次排查中，需要分清楚的是「啟動項」和「啟動檔案」。前者記錄在韌體的 NVRAM 中，告訴韌體到哪個分割區、哪條路徑載入程式；後者則是 EFI 分割區裡實際存在的 .efi 檔案。GRUB 檔案已經安裝成功，不代表韌體就會自動選中它。手動啟動成功，恰好讓這兩個問題暫時分開了。

當時採用的做法，是把已經驗證能夠啟動的 GRUB EFI 檔案，複製到 Windows Boot Manager 原有的位置：

這裡的 /efi 是 EFI 系統分割區在 Linux 中的掛載點。從韌體的角度看，目標檔案的路徑是 \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi。兩種寫法指向同一個位置，只是觀察它的環境不同。

當時執行的複製指令如下。這一步會直接覆寫目標檔案；以下保留的是事故中的操作記錄。

重新啟動後，韌體仍然走原來的 Windows 啟動路徑，但那個位置上的程式已經換成 GRUB。檔名仍是 bootmgfw.efi，內容卻不再是原來的 Windows Boot Manager。接著由 GRUB 載入 Arch，便繞過了自訂啟動項無法保留的障礙。

這只能說明，借用原有路徑確實讓 Arch 自動啟動了。自訂 NVRAM 啟動項為什麼消失，仍沒有查明；也不能僅憑這次經驗，就認定所有 HP 韌體都只能使用這條路徑。

代價也落在同一個位置：原路徑上的 Windows Boot Manager 被覆寫了。 當時是否另外保存了原始 bootmgfw.efi，現有記錄還不足以確認，因此不能把它寫成一次已經準備好回復方式的替換。若要恢復 Windows 的啟動鏈，需要從有效備份或 Windows 恢復環境恢復原始啟動檔案，並核對 BCD 啟動設定。微軟的 BCDBoot 文件說明了重建系統分割區啟動檔案和 BCD 的用途；具體操作仍要以恢復環境中實際辨識出的 Windows 分割區和 EFI 分割區為準。即使之後在 GRUB 選單中加入 Windows 項目，也必須確認它指向真正的 Windows 載入程式；原來那條路徑如今裝著的已經是 GRUB。

至於先前的 INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE，它仍然是另一個沒有解決的問題。韌體能載入 EFI 程式、Windows Boot Manager 能接續啟動流程，以及 Windows 核心能存取系統磁碟，是不同階段的檢查。這次替換改變了最前面的入口，並沒有修復後面的儲存裝置存取問題，也沒有解開或修復 BitLocker 系統分割區。

所以，這個結果只能記作「Arch 可以自動啟動」。Windows 的原始啟動檔案需要恢復，系統磁碟無法存取的原因也仍要獨立排查。到這裡，安裝取得了一個能用的入口，搶修卻還沒有結束。

暫時停在這裡

進入 Arch 後，又繼續設定 KDE Plasma、SDDM，以及日常開發環境。建立一般使用者，設定 wheel 群組的 sudo 權限，安裝終端機、檔案管理器和 Yakuake，再處理網路、藍牙和顯示卡驅動。

這不是一次完成的雙系統安裝。多出來的 Arch 可以使用，原有的 Windows 卻還沒有回來。最初省去的一個隨身碟，最後讓安裝媒體、故障系統和恢復入口，全都擠在同一塊磁碟上。

回想整個過程，我對 ChatGPT 的信任，逐漸超過了它實際掌握的資訊。它能解釋 GPT、UEFI 和 GRUB，也能把指令寫得完整，但眼前這塊磁碟的狀態，仍然需要一項一項核對。我把「回答得出下一步」當成了「已經確認上一步」，而這兩者之間的距離，最後要在自己的電腦上承擔。

以後再讓 AI 協助處理磁碟和啟動鏈，我會先停在唯讀檢查：目標是哪個裝置，現在裝著什麼，寫入會改變什麼，失敗後從哪裡恢復。分割區表和備份都應該在指令之前。

原本只是想多裝一個系統。最後留下的，是一個能啟動的 Arch，一個尚待恢復的 Windows，以及對「下一步」多一點的遲疑。

於是我突然非常想給我的 Windows PC 安裝上 Arch Linux 雙系統，正好我最近的研究任務也需要一個 Linux 環境。

手邊沒有隨身碟，於是打算直接從硬碟啟動安裝映像。具體思路是，建立一個臨時分割區作為安裝媒體，之後可以改作 swap 分割區。

從 Windows 分出約 150 GB，140 GB 留給 Arch，另外 10 GB 暫時充當安裝媒體。

直到 Windows 在重新啟動後，留給我一行 INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE。

entry.title: When the Answer Arrives Late: Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs
entry.content:
A language model may already know which word it will write before it reaches its last layer. If so, the remaining layers look like an opportunity: stop early, emit the token, and spend less computation on a decision that has already been made.

The difficulty is knowing when a decision is finished. A plausible intermediate answer can still change. And as models improve, the work that once seemed redundant may become part of what makes the answer correct.

This is the question behind Rui Wei and colleagues’ The Diminishing Returns of Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs. Their experiments suggest that many newer models offer surprisingly little room for straightforward early exit, even when an experimental oracle can inspect the final answer before choosing an exit. The useful contribution is a way to examine that room before building a system around it. Paper, arXiv v1

What it means to leave a model early

Consider a decoder with $L$ layers. For each generated token, it transforms a hidden representation through those layers and uses a language-model head to produce scores over the vocabulary. These scores are called logits. A decoding rule then selects the next token.

An early-exit decoder tries to make that selection at some intermediate layer $\ell<L$. It needs both an intermediate prediction and a rule for deciding whether that prediction is trustworthy enough.

At first glance, common words and punctuation seem likely to require less work than a difficult reasoning step. But “easy to predict” and “stable halfway through this particular model” are different properties. The model may use late layers to change a token’s ranking, adjust its confidence, or incorporate information that earlier layers have not resolved.

Autoregressive generation also carries mistakes forward. Once an early-exit token enters the sequence, the next prediction is conditioned on it. A small local change can become a different reasoning path several tokens later.

The paper therefore asks two connected questions: do intermediate layers resemble the final layer closely enough to support early exit, and does that resemblance survive an end-to-end task evaluation? Its focus is the model’s existing behavior under little or no extra training. Sections 2–3

Three ways to ask whether a layer is ready

The authors compare intermediate and final layers through three signals:

SignalWhat is comparedWhat it helps reveal
Hidden statesIntermediate and final representationsWhether the internal representation has become similar to its final form
LogitsVocabulary scores from the shared language-model headWhether intermediate predictions resemble the final scores
Top-10 candidatesThe leading token candidates at each depthWhether the set of plausible next tokens has stabilized

These signals describe different kinds of agreement. Similar hidden states need not produce the same next token. Two candidate sets can overlap while their first-ranked tokens differ. And similar logit vectors need not preserve the ranking of two nearly tied candidates.

There is a further distinction worth keeping visible: logits are not probabilities. Softmax converts logits into probabilities. Cosine similarity between raw score vectors is a useful probe, but it is neither a calibrated confidence measure nor a guarantee that the resulting distributions or chosen tokens match.

Across the models examined, many similarity curves rise meaningfully only near the end of the network. Llama2-7B shows earlier alignment than several newer models, while GPT-OSS-20B is a notable exception with relatively early logit alignment. Qwen2-7B shows low or negative logit similarity over much of its depth. The paper’s Figure 4 makes these differences more apparent than a single aggregate score can. Section 4.1

A score for the available room

Exiting one layer before the end may preserve quality but save little work. Exiting halfway through may save many layers but produce an unreliable answer. The authors combine these two considerations in an early-exit adaptability score, or EAS.

The fraction of layers skipped by an exit at layer $\ell$ is

They measure layer-to-final cosine similarity as

where $\mathbf{x}$ represents the signal being compared. After linearly mapping similarity into the interval $[0,1]$, giving $\widetilde S_\ell$, the per-layer score is

The model-level score averages over candidate exit layers:

For $0<\alpha<1$, the geometric mean rewards a layer that offers both similarity and savings. The parameter $\alpha$ controls the balance. The authors ultimately use logit similarity as the central signal after comparing its relationship with task accuracy. Sections 3.3 and 4.2

As an illustration, suppose a 32-layer model exits after layer 24. Its skip ratio is 0.25. If mapped similarity is 0.90 and we choose $\alpha=0.5$ for this example, its per-layer score is $\sqrt{0.90\times0.25}\approx0.474$. This is a teaching example, not a reported measurement or a claim about the paper’s experimental choice of $\alpha$.

EAS is a screening metric. An EAS of 0.52 does not mean 52% of layers can safely be skipped, and it does not mean a 1.52× speedup. Averaging also hides the exact location of useful exits. A deployment decision still needs the layer curves and the task-level trade-off.

Giving the exit rule knowledge it cannot normally have

A practical exit rule cannot compare its current logits with the final layer’s logits without computing the final layer. The paper temporarily removes this obstacle through an oracle experiment.

For each token, the oracle runs the full model, obtains intermediate predictions, and selects the earliest layer whose similarity to the final logits exceeds a threshold $\delta$. It then generates the token from that selected layer. The sequence continues using those selected tokens, so the task evaluation includes the consequences of changed generation.

Appendix C describes this procedure. A simplified reading is:

This is an experiment about potential savings. The oracle actually computes the full depth. Its recorded skip ratio describes the layers an exit would have avoided if the needed information were available for free. It is not a measured reduction in runtime.

The oracle also has limits as an “upper bound.” It uses a particular similarity criterion and a threshold search. It offers unusually informed decisions within that setup, but it does not prove a universal maximum over all possible exit policies, retrained models, or speculative methods. Section 4.3 and Appendix C

How little survives the accuracy constraint

The benchmark uses OpenCompass, zero-shot evaluation, temperature zero, and a default maximum of 1,024 output tokens. The broader similarity study covers MMLU, GSM8K, GPQA, and HumanEval, using fixed subsets of 100 prompts per dataset with the same sampling seed across models.

For the oracle results, the authors search for thresholds that maximize skipping while keeping accuracy loss within their stated “5%” budget. The table below reformats their Table 1. Accuracy values have been converted from fractions to percentages; skip ratios are already percentages.

ModelMMLU accuracy, full → exitMMLU layers skippedGSM8K accuracy, full → exitGSM8K layers skippedEAS
Llama2-7B41% → 38%4.69%21% → 17%2.13%0.52
Llama3-8B54% → 52%0.18%37% → 33%0.04%0.46
Llama4-Scout76% → 73%0.32%85% → 82%0.18%0.47
Qwen2-7B24% → 24%0.00%53% → 53%0.00%0.36
Qwen3-8B41% → 39%0.10%54% → 51%0.62%0.51
GPT-OSS-20B74% → 69%7.26%61% → 57%4.48%0.59

Source: Wei et al., Table 1. The displayed losses fit a budget of five percentage points. They do not all fit a 5% relative-loss budget: for example, 21% to 17% is a four-point drop but about a 19% relative reduction. This distinction matters when interpreting the paper’s wording.

The striking result is the size of the usable window. Llama3-8B skips just 0.18% of layers on MMLU and 0.04% on GSM8K. Qwen2-7B reaches zero savings in both reported settings. GPT-OSS-20B offers more room, but even its best value here is 7.26%.

Suppose, purely as a cost model, every layer took the same time and all other work were free. Skipping a fraction $s$ of layers would give a speedup of $1/(1-s)$. At $s=0.0726$, that is about 1.078×. At $s=0.0018$, it is about 1.0018×. These are illustrative calculations from the reported skip ratios, not latency results from the paper.

Real execution adds exit checks, intermediate vocabulary projections, memory traffic, and scheduling. Token-dependent exits also have to coexist with batched serving and the attention cache: when an earlier token skips deeper layers, a later token may still need their cached keys and values. Any missing state needs a handling strategy. Those costs make skip ratio a starting point for systems work, rather than its conclusion.

What changes the opportunity

The paper examines four factors. Together they suggest that early-exit potential belongs to a particular trained model, rather than following automatically from its parameter count or architecture name. Section 5

Scale. Larger models generally have higher EAS in the studied families, although the curves are not uniformly monotonic. More capacity can leave more room for similar intermediate predictions. That does not imply a larger model with early exit will be cheaper than a smaller model evaluated at full depth.

Architecture. A representative comparison gives EAS values of 0.51 for dense Qwen3-8B, 0.49 for Qwen3-30B-A3B, and 0.48 for Mamba-Codestral-7B. The authors interpret the dense model’s smoother alignment as offering more opportunity than the selected MoE and state-space models. But these checkpoints differ in size and training as well as architecture. GPT-OSS-20B, itself an MoE, also has the highest EAS in Table 1. The evidence supports a pattern in the selected comparisons, not a rule excluding MoE from useful early exit.

Training. Released Pythia-12B checkpoints let the authors inspect representation changes during pretraining. Later training produces a middle-layer region with lower similarity to the final layer. A separate Qwen3-4B base-versus-instruction comparison shows delayed logit alignment after instruction tuning. The proposed explanation is increasing specialization and late-layer calibration. Pythia gives a useful window into this process, but one training trajectory cannot establish the behavior of every model family.

Workload. Qwen3-8B’s layer curves have broadly similar shapes across the four datasets. This suggests a substantial model-level component to the pattern. It does not make task choice irrelevant: a multiple-choice answer, a numerical result, and executable code have different sensitivities to changed tokens and different evaluation rules.

The title’s “diminishing returns” should also be read as an empirical tendency. Qwen3-8B’s EAS of 0.51 is above Qwen2-7B’s 0.36 and close to Llama2-7B’s 0.52. GPT-OSS-20B reaches 0.59. The results do not trace a smooth decline with every release.

What I would take into an implementation

My engineering reading is that measurement should precede the exit controller. For a chosen checkpoint and workload, I would first inspect intermediate predictions, then measure the task-accuracy curve under an optimistic exit policy. Only after finding meaningful room would I build a practical predictor and measure actual latency and throughput.

The accuracy budget should be explicit in percentage points or relative loss. Threshold selection should use separate calibration data, followed by evaluation on held-out examples. With 100 prompts, one changed answer moves accuracy by one percentage point; a narrow margin deserves more evidence than a single small sample can supply.

There are also two different projects to distinguish. One tries to exploit intermediate predictions that already exist. Another changes training so useful predictions emerge earlier, using auxiliary heads, early-exit objectives, or an early-exit draft verified by a fuller model. This paper mainly tests the first project’s assumptions. Its limitations section explicitly leaves room for methods that alter the model. Conclusion and limitations

I would treat EAS as a reason to investigate, then inspect the accuracy-versus-skip frontier directly. A single scalar can rank candidates approximately; it cannot choose a serving policy or account for hardware costs.

Depth has to earn its removal

Early exit begins with an appealing thought: perhaps the answer arrives before the computation ends. The paper asks us to test that thought against the layers themselves, and then against the generated sequence.

For many of the studied models, the trustworthy answer arrives late. Their improvement may have consumed some of the slack that earlier acceleration methods depended on. In that setting, removing depth means removing work that is still shaping the prediction.

There is still a useful question to carry forward: at what point does this model, on this workload, have enough information to stop? The answer belongs to measurement. An optimization becomes convincing when the computation it removes has demonstrably finished its job.

This article is an explanatory reading, not an independent reproduction of the experiments. Reported measurements come from Rui Wei, Rui Du, Hanfei Yu, Devesh Tiwari, Jian Li, Zhaozhuo Xu, and Hao Wang, The Diminishing Returns of Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs, arXiv:2603.23701v1 (March 24, 2026). The cost examples and implementation recommendations are my interpretation. Original PDF · HTML text · alphaXiv
entry.summary: A reading of early-exit decoding in modern LLMs: layer similarity, oracle skip ratios, training effects, and the gap between skipped computation and real speed.

entry.title: How Close Is FlashAttention to the Limit? Understanding Attention Through Data Movement
entry.content:
Reading Barna Saha and Christopher Ye, The I/O Complexity of Attention, or How Optimal is Flash Attention? (2024). Original paper

We often measure an algorithm’s cost in FLOPs. On a GPU, however, less arithmetic does not necessarily mean less time: arithmetic units may be waiting for data to travel from device memory to on-chip storage. FlashAttention’s central contribution is to reduce that movement. This paper asks a further question: how much room remains?

The answer depends on the memory regime. In the paper’s large-cache model, FlashAttention already achieves the optimal asymptotic I/O complexity. With a small cache, a different tiling strategy does better. Optimality here concerns the order of data movement, rather than the fastest possible implementation.

Attention as a mathematical problem

For a single attention head, let

Here $N$ is the sequence length and $d$ the head dimension. The score between query $i$ and key $j$ is

Actual models usually divide this score by $\sqrt d$. That scaling does not change the I/O orders discussed here, so we omit it.

Softmax turns each row of scores into weights:

The output is a weighted average:

In matrix form,

Computing both products with classical matrix multiplication takes roughly $4N^2d$ FLOPs, counting multiplication and addition separately and ignoring lower-order terms. Yet the intermediate score matrix has $N^2$ entries, while the output has only $Nd$. Must we store that enormous intermediate matrix?

Two memory levels: a warehouse and a workbench

The paper uses an idealized model. Slow memory is large; fast memory holds only $M$ numbers. All computation happens in fast memory, and each number loaded or stored counts as one I/O operation.

On a GPU, we can think of the slow level as device memory and the fast level as on-chip storage. Real hardware has registers, shared memory, and multiple cache levels; the model abstracts one boundary within that hierarchy.

The units matter. $M$ counts elements, rather than bytes. If fast memory holds $C$ bytes and each element occupies $w$ bytes, then

Moving $L$ elements means transferring $wL$ bytes. The paper seeks the smallest possible asymptotic order of $L$, rather than directly predicting seconds.

Softmax without storing the score matrix

Fix one query and define

Then its output is $o=u/z$. We can process keys and values block by block, adding each block’s contributions to $z$ and $u$ without retaining every score.

For numerical stability, implementations also maintain a maximum $m$ and use

If the new block’s score indices form a set $J$, update the maximum to

The existing accumulators must be rescaled:

The final output remains $o=u/\ell$. These equations explain why score computation can be fused with accumulation and the score blocks discarded. They are background for understanding FlashAttention, rather than new contributions of this lower-bound paper. Exact attention means evaluating the same mathematical function; changing floating-point execution order can still change rounding.

Large caches: where FlashAttention’s I/O comes from

Let $B$ be the number of queries in a fast-memory block. Each query needs $d$ elements, alongside output accumulators and temporary storage. Ignoring constants,

One intuitive schedule keeps a query block and its output state in fast memory, then scans all of $K,V$. Each scan costs $\Theta(Nd)$, and there are about $N/B$ query blocks. The leading term is therefore

As a teaching example, take $N=4096,d=64,M=65536$ elements.

These are values of asymptotic expressions, rather than exact load and store counts. Actual block sizes must reserve room for accumulators, temporary scores, and other state. The example illustrates the scaling: in this regime, doubling fast memory can roughly halve the leading movement term.

The paper proves a matching lower bound for the classical matrix multiplication model when $M\ge d^2$. This is more than a convenient tiling strategy: alternative schedules cannot improve its asymptotic order.

Small caches: when storing an intermediate matrix helps

When $M\lt d^2$, tiling around whole vectors of dimension $d$ is too restrictive. Instead, use square blocks with side length

so that two input blocks and an output block fit in fast memory. A local product uses $\Theta(b^2)$ elements to support $\Theta(b^3)$ scalar multiply-adds, giving reuse efficiency $\Theta(b)=\Theta(\sqrt M)$.

The two attention products require $\Theta(N^2d)$ multiply-adds in total, so this strategy achieves

It writes the exponentiated score matrix to slow memory, consuming $\Theta(N^2)$ space. But the small-cache condition implies

Writing $N^2$ elements therefore does not increase the asymptotic leading term. Never storing an intermediate matrix is not a universally optimal rule.

Compare the two strategies:

For $M\lt d^2$, the ratio exceeds one and square tiling moves less data. For $M\gt d^2$, FlashAttention-style fused tiling does better. The crossover is precisely $M=d^2$.

Putting the regimes together

Theorem 3.1 gives the following leading term for classical matrix multiplication:

For ordinary attention dimensions, including compulsory input and output traffic, it is useful to understand this as

The added $Nd$ emphasizes the cost of reading inputs and writing outputs. With an extremely large cache, the leading-term expression cannot be extrapolated to traffic smaller than the output itself. Here we assume the common regime $d\le N$; extreme rectangular shapes require explicit checks of block dimensions and compulsory I/O.

Fast-memory regimeSuitable strategyLeading movement term
$M\lt d^2$Square matrix multiplication tiles; store the intermediate matrix$N^2d/\sqrt M$
$M\ge d^2$Fused streaming accumulation; avoid the full score matrix$N^2d^2/M$

Proving a lower bound for a fixed computation graph

The red-blue pebble game represents dependencies as a DAG. Inputs and intermediate values are vertices, and dependencies are edges. Red pebbles represent values in fast memory, with at most $M$ available; blue pebbles represent values in slow memory.

There is no need to enumerate every schedule. Divide an execution into phases of $M$ I/O operations, then ask how many scores one phase can complete.

In the large-cache regime, the paper proves that a phase can complete only

entries of $QK^\top$. Intuitively, each query or key vector requires $d$ elements. About $M/d$ queries and $M/d$ keys can form only about $(M/d)^2$ pairs.

A rigorous proof must also handle partially computed dot products. Counting complete vectors alone is insufficient. The paper analyzes summation trees and partition boundaries to account for these partial computations.

There are $N^2$ scores, so at least $\Omega(N^2d^2/M^2)$ phases are needed. Multiplying by the $\Theta(M)$ movement budget per phase gives

What if we use a Strassen-like algorithm?

A proof for a fixed DAG does not automatically rule out another matrix multiplication algorithm: changing the algorithm changes the graph. The paper’s second part addresses this distinction.

The authors introduce a communication problem called matrix entry compression. Alice knows the input matrices and sends Bob a short message. Bob must recover $B$ entries of their product. If those entries contain substantial independent information, the message cannot be arbitrarily short.

The key communication lower bound has the form

measured in finite-field elements. An I/O phase has an information budget of only $O(M)$ elements, so it can produce at most

product entries. This yields the lower bound in Theorem 4.8:

When $M\ge d^2$, this matches FlashAttention’s leading term. The proof uses a finite field $\mathbb F_q$ with $q\gt N$ and constructions based on linear independence. The corresponding binary-input result loses logarithmic factors. It cannot be applied without qualification as an information-theoretic theorem for arbitrary floating-point representations.

The scope also matters: the extension allows different matrix multiplication methods while still computing entries of $QK^\top$. It is not an unrestricted lower bound for every conceivable attention algorithm that might bypass those explicit entries, use approximation, or exploit special inputs.

For small caches, the authors connect attention to the I/O complexity of rectangular matrix multiplication. Once fast matrix multiplication is allowed, the paper does not supply one tight closed-form expression covering every case.

From a movement lower bound to a performance upper bound

The following is an application of the paper to performance modeling. If at least $L_{\min}$ elements must cross a memory boundary, each occupies $w$ bytes, and that boundary has a bandwidth ceiling $\beta$, then

If the chosen algorithm class also requires at least $F_{\min}$ FLOPs, and the compute ceiling at the relevant precision is $P$, then

Taking the maximum allows ideal overlap between computation and transfer. This is an optimistic time lower bound, rather than a prediction of actual runtime. An asymptotic $\Omega$ expression alone also supplies no reliable numerical constant.

For a Bound Estimator on a Mac, first specify the memory boundary, effective capacity, precision, and algorithm class. Unified memory does not eliminate movement between on-chip storage and DRAM.

The paper studies full $N\times N$ attention. Single-token decoding has query length one, so its cost cannot be obtained by copying an $N^2$ formula. It needs rectangular analysis and a separate account of where the existing KV state resides.

What remains after reading the paper?

FlashAttention lets a score complete its entire purpose in fast memory: it is generated, participates in normalization and weighted accumulation, then disappears. The lower-bound paper shows that, in the specified model’s large-cache regime, this strategy reaches the asymptotic limit of data movement.

There is still distance between optimal movement and minimum runtime. Parallelism, instruction throughput, synchronization, register occupancy, and constant factors remain open to improvement. Theory is most useful when it tells us where an improvement in asymptotic order is still possible, and where the next gains must come from implementation efficiency.

Where to read in the original

  • Pages 4–6: two-level memory, red-blue pebbling, and the partition lemma.
  • Pages 7–13, Theorems 3.1, 3.2, and 3.5: large- and small-cache results for classical matrix multiplication.
  • Pages 14–20, Theorems 4.8 and 4.14: communication complexity and broader matrix multiplication algorithms.
  • Page 21, Theorem 4.17 and the conclusion: rectangular matrix multiplication in the small-cache regime and open questions.

This is an original exposition. Online softmax, numerical examples, and hardware performance conversions provide intuition; the original paper determines each theorem’s precise scope.

entry.title: Beyond FLOPs: How COSMA Builds Parallel Matrix Multiplication from Communication Bounds
entry.content:
Reading Grzegorz Kwasniewski et al., Red-blue pebbling revisited: near optimal parallel matrix-matrix multiplication (2019, arXiv v3). Original paper

Suppose a matrix multiplication requires a trillion multiply-adds. Adding processors seems as though it should keep shortening the runtime. Yet each processor must receive its inputs, and partial results from different processors may need to be combined. As arithmetic gets faster, movement can become the bottleneck.

COSMA begins with a question: what reuse does finite memory permit? It then seeks a work decomposition with as little communication as possible and turns that decomposition into parallel matrix multiplication.

Its focus is classical matrix multiplication, where each output is an ordinary sum of products. The same optimality claim does not include Strassen-like algorithms.

Three indices form a three-dimensional computation space

Let

Each output entry is

A scalar multiply-add corresponds to a triple $(i,j,\ell)$. The whole computation can therefore be pictured as an $m\times n\times k$ box containing $mnk$ multiply-add positions.

Suppose a processor receives an $a\times b\times c$ sub-box. The three data sets it needs are exactly the projections of that box onto three coordinate planes:

DataLocal shapeElements
$A$$a\times c$$ac$
$B$$c\times b$$bc$
Partial sums of $C$$a\times b$$ab$

The local work is $abc$, and the boundary volume of inputs and final local outputs is $ac+bc+ab$. A large computation volume with a small boundary means substantial reuse.

Why a square root appears in the lower bound

Let fast memory hold $S$ elements. If three square tiles of side length $t$ all reside there, then

Loading $\Theta(t^2)$ numbers supports $\Theta(t^3)$ multiply-adds. Each transferred number supports $\Theta(t)$ multiply-adds, so the reuse scales as $\sqrt S$, rather than $S$.

The whole multiplication has $mnk$ multiply-adds. The leading term of the classical I/O lower bound is therefore

This square-tile example explains the exponent $1/2$, but does not prove a bound for all schedules. A rigorous proof must handle irregular tiles, partial sums, recomputation, and reuse across phases.

COSMA starts from red-blue pebbling and graph partitions to make the reuse analysis more precise, paying particular attention to constants hidden by asymptotic notation.

A better sequential schedule: retain outputs and stream inputs

Keeping three large tiles simultaneously is not the only strategy. We can retain an $a\times b$ output tile in fast memory while streaming column segments of $A$ and row segments of $B$ through it.

For a fixed $\ell$, the update is an outer product:

Reading $a+b$ numbers completes $ab$ multiply-adds, giving reuse efficiency

For a fixed output area $ab=R$, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives

so efficiency is greatest at $a=b=\sqrt R$:

Most of the memory should therefore hold an output tile as close to square as possible, supported by smaller input buffers.

Each output tile is written only after traversing the full $k$ dimension. Ignoring edges, divisibility, and buffer space, tiles with side length roughly $\sqrt S$ give leading input traffic

Add $mn$ elements for the final output. This explains the coefficient 2 that the paper studies closely, and why repeatedly writing partial sums wastes communication.

In a real schedule, not all $S$ positions can hold output: inputs and newly computed values also need space. The paper explicitly handles this executability constraint. Its near-optimal factor has the form

which approaches one as $S$ grows. A figure such as 0.03% describes closeness to a communication guarantee within the model; it does not mean runtime is within 0.03% of hardware peak performance.

From fixed partitions to proofs that account for reuse

The classical Hong–Kung argument cuts an execution by I/O count and uses partition boundaries to limit the work in each phase. COSMA further distinguishes values already resident at phase entry, values that must be newly loaded, and results that must be saved.

Its reuse lemma uses $X$ as the partition parameter, $R(S)$ as an upper bound on the reuse set, and $T(S)$ as a lower bound on necessary stores, obtaining

where $H(X)$ is the minimum number of subcomputations in a valid partition.

This is more precise than simply assigning $S$ transfers to every phase. Existing values can be reused, but all of fast memory cannot simultaneously be reserved for reuse while additional inputs occupy space outside that budget. Executability must be counted too.

The paper first analyzes greedy schedules that reuse data promptly, then argues that non-greedy schedules cannot beat the corresponding lower bound. Greedy has a formal definition here; it does not mean an arbitrary local heuristic.

Any concrete bound also requires checking the input/output convention and dimension regime. Traffic changes if inputs already occupy the target memory level, or the entire problem fits there. Usually we should also check the compulsory cost

under the usual convention that inputs start in slow memory and outputs must be written back. The communication leading term cannot be extrapolated indefinitely without these conditions.

When should parallel multiplication split the third dimension?

The argument still assumes classical matrix multiplication. Independence from an existing implementation does not eliminate algorithmic assumptions.

If several Transformer matrix multiplications are fused, one operator’s output may remain in fast memory for the next. We cannot mechanically add compulsory writeback costs for isolated operators. The lower bound must describe the permitted fusion scope and residency state.

COSMA’s central idea becomes a concrete question: how should this memory be organized so that every transferred number participates in as much useful computation as possible? Answering that before selecting a fixed processor grid gives the decomposition a reason to exist.

The outer-product derivation and numerical examples are original explanations. The local geometric model builds intuition; strict guarantees require the paper’s machine and computation assumptions.

Suppose a matrix multiplication requires a trillion multiply-adds. Adding processors seems as though it should keep shortening the runtime. Yet each processor must receive its inputs, and partial results from different processors may need to be combined. As arithmetic gets faster, movement can become the bottleneck.

COSMA begins with a question: what reuse does finite memory permit? It then seeks a work decomposition with as little communication as possible and turns that decomposition into parallel matrix multiplication.

Its focus is classical matrix multiplication, where each output is an ordinary sum of products. The same optimality claim does not include Strassen-like algorithms.

entry.title: The Red-Blue Pebble Game: Why Faster Processors Still Have to Move Data
entry.content:
Reading Jia-Wei Hong and H. T. Kung, I/O Complexity: The Red-Blue Pebble Game, STOC 1981, pp. 326–333. Original paper

Imagine an infinitely fast processor whose workbench holds only ten numbers. To process a million numbers, it still has to bring them in from storage. Intermediate results that do not fit must travel out, and perhaps return later.

This 1981 paper studies exactly that limitation. A simple game turns the movement caused by finite fast memory into a mathematical problem with provable bounds. Later work on communication-optimal matrix multiplication and attention I/O follows the same line of thought.

From an expression to a computation graph

Consider

The dependencies form a DAG:

A vertex represents a value or the operation producing it; an edge represents a dependency. We cannot compute $y$ without $u,v$.

The graph specifies which computations must happen, but neither their execution order nor which intermediate values remain in memory. Different schedules can evaluate the same graph with different amounts of movement.

Two pebble colors, two storage levels

A red pebble means a value is in fast memory; a blue pebble means it is in slow memory. A vertex may carry both colors, representing a copy at each level.

There are at most $S$ red pebbles, while slow memory is unbounded. Inputs begin in slow memory, and final outputs must also be saved there.

OperationGame ruleComputer interpretationCounts as I/O?
LoadPlace a red pebble on a vertex carrying a blue pebbleRead from slow to fast memoryYes
StorePlace a blue pebble on a vertex carrying a red pebbleWrite from fast to slow memoryYes
ComputePlace a red pebble on a result only when all immediate predecessors carry red pebblesExecute an operation with its inputs readyNo
DeleteRemove a pebbleFree a storage positionNo

The goal is to finish the outputs while minimizing the total number of loads and stores:

We use $L$ for I/O count to avoid confusion with attention’s query matrix $Q$; the original paper uses $Q$.

One pebble represents one word. Converting traffic to bytes requires specifying the word width.

Playing the game by hand

Return to the expression above with $S=4$. Load $a,b$, compute $u$, then remove $a,b$. Load $c,d$, compute $v$, then remove $c,d$. Compute $y$ and finally store it.

Each of the four inputs is read once, and the output is written once: five I/O operations. At most four values coexist, namely $u,c,d,v$.

With less capacity, we may need to spill $u$ to slow memory and reload it later, adding one store and one load. Another possibility is to discard $u$, then reload $a,b$ and recompute it when needed.

The original game permits recomputation: its computation rule does not require each vertex to be evaluated only once. This allows a trade between extra arithmetic and less storage. Some later models forbid recomputation, so a lower bound must be read with its model version in mind.

Why not search every possible play?

Small graphs can be enumerated, but the number of legal schedules grows rapidly. Rather than finding the best play for every DAG, Hong and Kung ask a static question: how many subcomputations with bounded boundaries are needed to partition this graph?

If each subcomputation can perform only limited work, a large problem needs many phases. More phases force more movement.

This is a proof technique. It establishes costs no legal execution can avoid, but does not automatically produce an optimal program.

Where the factor 2S comes from

Cut an execution into consecutive phases, each complete phase containing exactly $S$ I/O operations. The last phase may contain fewer.

At phase entry, fast memory contains at most $S$ values, and the phase can load at most $S$ more. Its supporting boundary information is therefore at most $2S$. At phase exit, at most $S$ values remain in fast memory, and at most $S$ can have been stored, so the output boundary is also at most $2S$.

This induces a $2S$-partition. The original definition requires four properties: disjoint parts covering the whole graph, a small dominator set for each part, a small minimum set for each part, and no cyclic dependencies between parts.

A dominator set is a collection of unavoidable entrances: every path from an input to a vertex in the part passes through it. It need not coincide with array elements directly read by source code.

The minimum set consists of vertices in a part with no successor remaining in that part. These are exits of the internal computation; minimum does not refer to numerical values.

This phase argument explains $2S$, but the rigorous construction must handle recomputed vertices. Occurrences during execution cannot simply be declared disjoint parts of a static graph.

The central lemma

Let $P(G,2S)$ be the smallest number of parts among valid $2S$-partitions. Lemma 3.1 states

Why subtract one? The final phase need not consume all $S$ I/O operations.

Suppose the graph contains $W$ computation vertices being counted, and each legal part contains at most $U(2S)$. Then

Substituting gives

This is a practical proof template: bound the work supported by a finite boundary, then divide total work by that bound. The difficulty usually lies in bounding $U(S)$, rather than enumerating schedules.

Matrix multiplication: why n³/√S transfers are necessary

Classical $n\times n$ matrix multiplication requires $n^3$ scalar multiplications:

A subset of these multiplications can be represented as a set of triples $T\subseteq\lbrace(i,j,k)\rbrace$. Its projections onto the three coordinate planes correspond to the entries of $A$, $B$, and the partial sums of $C$ that it uses.

A modern geometric explanation uses a discrete Loomis–Whitney-type inequality:

If each projection contains only $O(S)$ elements, then

A subcomputation constrained by that memory boundary thus supports only $O(S^{3/2})$ useful multiplications. At least

subcomputations are required. Multiplying by the $S$-operation I/O budget per phase yields

The projection inequality explains the exponent; it is not a claim that the original paper uses this proof language. Section 6 derives the ordinary matrix multiplication result through independent computations and counting. A formal proof cannot equate the number of values currently in fast memory with an entire phase’s boundary.

The rectangular version is

under the corresponding computation and dimension assumptions. If inputs start in slow memory and outputs must be written back, compulsory I/O also matters. A common asymptotic expression is

with the memory and rectangular-dimension regime checked explicitly. Even a large memory must read inputs and write outputs.

Can the lower bound be attained?

Use square tiles of side length $b=\Theta(\sqrt S)$. Two input tiles and one output tile require $\Theta(b^2)$ fast-memory space, and each local product completes $\Theta(b^3)$ multiply-adds.

There are approximately $(n/b)^3$ tile products, each requiring $O(b^2)$ traffic, giving

The upper and lower bounds match in order, so the square-root relation reflects a real limitation. Quadrupling memory roughly halves the leading communication term; doubling it improves that term by only about $\sqrt2$.

Why FFT has log S instead

The FFT graph has $\Theta(n\log n)$ computation vertices. The paper shows that a part with boundary size $O(S)$ contains at most $O(S\log S)$ vertices. Thus

In the usual regime $2\le S\le n$, a suitable decomposition achieves the same order. Intuitively, a local FFT of size $S$ can complete about $\log S$ layers while resident in fast memory. The whole graph has about $\log n$ layers and therefore needs repeated movement across the boundary.

Matrix multiplication and FFT have different reuse structures, so increased capacity benefits them differently. One rule for how much doubling memory improves performance cannot describe every algorithm.

Other graphs in the paper

The paper also analyzes information propagation speed, odd-even transposition sorting networks, snake-like meshes, and graph products.

For example, a local region of scale $r$ in a $d$-dimensional directed mesh has roughly $r^d$ vertices but needs roughly $r^{d-1}$ boundary information. If that boundary is limited by $S$, then

For the corresponding graph with $m^d$ vertices, this relationship leads to a related I/O lower bound of

The original paper establishes this using a graph-product theorem for dominators. The volume-and-boundary argument above provides intuition. This discussion assumes $d\gt 1$, as required by the exponents.

A common theme emerges: the geometry of dependencies determines how much work a small workbench can sustain.

From I/O lower bounds to hardware performance limits

The following applies the paper to modern performance estimation. If at least $L_{\min}$ words must move, each occupies $w$ bytes, and the relevant boundary has bandwidth ceiling $\beta$, then

If the specified algorithm also needs at least $F_{\min}$ FLOPs and hardware peak compute at the matching precision is $P$, then

This connects a movement lower bound to Roofline. An optimistic time lower bound can be derived without measuring an existing kernel’s actual traffic.

For example, if a bound with proven numerical constants requires at least 8 GB of movement and the bandwidth ceiling is 400 GB/s, runtime is at least 20 ms. If the task generates $R$ tokens, the corresponding throughput upper bound is $R/0.020$ tokens per second.

An $\Omega(\cdot)$ expression without usable constants cannot be treated as an exact byte count. The compute peak must also match the operation type and precision.

What exactly is optimal?

The most important qualification is that the red-blue pebble game starts from a given computation graph.

Within that graph, we can change execution order, tiling, residency, and even allow recomputation. A different mathematical algorithm may have an entirely different graph. A lower bound for ordinary matrix multiplication does not automatically rule out Strassen. A bound for one attention graph does not automatically constrain approximate attention.

We can say that every legal schedule of this DAG obeys the bound. A claim about every algorithm solving the underlying problem requires a specified algorithm class or stronger algebraic, communication, or information-theoretic arguments.

The game also leaves many hardware constraints outside the model: SIMD width, Tensor Core instruction shapes, parallelism, synchronization, cache-line granularity, and multiple memory levels. It captures movement limits rather than simulating a complete machine.

Using the result in a Bound Estimator

First fix the model and workload, then specify permitted transformations: operator fusion, recomputation, approximation, quantization, and the memory level where inputs and KV state already reside.

For that scope, establish a DAG or algorithm class, prove necessary computation and communication, and map them to hardware resources. If operators can be fused, their isolated writeback lower bounds cannot simply be added: intermediate data may never leave fast memory.

The resulting theoretical limit then has a precise meaning. The value of the red-blue pebble game is to make the claim that every kernel must move this much data something we can inspect, prove, and challenge by examining its assumptions.

Where to read in the original

  • Printed page 327, Section 2: game rules and the two-level storage interpretation.
  • Printed pages 328–329, Section 3: partitions, Theorem 3.1, and the central Lemma 3.1.
  • Section 4: the FFT lower bound.
  • Sections 5–6: information propagation and independent computations; Corollary 6.2 gives the ordinary rectangular matrix multiplication lower bound.
  • Sections 7–8: graph products, the decomposability factor, and the conclusion.

PDF page 1 corresponds to printed page 326. This is an original exposition; the projection inequality, worked example, and modern hardware conversions are explanations rather than a sentence-by-sentence translation of the paper.

entry.title: Git Needs a Trash Can
entry.content:
In a 2017 VS Code issue, someone described clicking Discard Changes after seeing roughly five thousand files in the Source Control view. They said the action removed their files, including work they could not find in the Recycle Bin. A screenshot of the issue circulated again, this time described as a pull request. It was an issue, but the distinction does not make the failure less interesting. My first reaction was short: we need git trash.

The name is slightly misleading. This is less about adding another verb to Git than about a missing promise in our tools: before a tool destroys local work, it should know how to give that work back.

What Git Can Actually Recover

Git gives us several places where a file can exist. They look similar in an editor’s Source Control panel, but they have very different recovery properties.

  1. Committed content is in the repository’s history. If a tracked file is deleted or changed, we can usually restore its committed version.
  2. Staged content has been copied into the index. It may differ from both the working file and the last commit.
  3. Unstaged content lives in the working tree. Git can show a diff against the index, but the current bytes have not necessarily been saved as a Git object.
  4. Untracked content is only a file on disk as far as ordinary Git history is concerned. git status can tell us that it exists; that does not mean Git has a copy.

This is why “it’s in a Git repository” is a poor synonym for “it’s backed up.” A three-month-old file that was never added may be less recoverable than a file committed five minutes ago. git restore can reconstruct content from the index or a commit. It cannot reconstruct bytes that Git never recorded. git clean, meanwhile, removes untracked files from the working tree; its -n option only previews that removal.

An editor compresses these different states into one list of changes. That is convenient for staging, but dangerous for deletion. The word “discard” can mean “restore this tracked file from the index” or “remove this untracked file from disk.” The UI may look like one operation while the consequences are not the same.

What a Trash Operation Would Need to Save

A useful git trash would be a recoverable discard, not simply an alias for git clean.

Before changing the working tree, it would capture the exact state being removed: file contents, paths, and whether each file was tracked, staged, untracked, or ignored. It would then record a durable recovery entry and only perform the discard after that entry had been written successfully. If saving fails, deletion should fail too.

Recovery also has to be selective. I might want one deleted file back without restoring every other change from that afternoon. If a new file now occupies the old path, the tool should report a conflict and offer a different destination instead of silently overwriting it. A useful entry would show when the discard happened, which paths it affected, and how much data it saved.

There are hard edges here. Repositories can contain gigabytes of generated files; ignored paths can hold secrets; a remote development environment may not have a desktop Recycle Bin. A trash system needs explicit size limits, retention rules, and clear handling for those cases. “Moved to Trash” should never be displayed when the bytes were actually deleted permanently.

This is also why an operating-system Trash is only a partial answer. It can help with an untracked file that is removed as a file. A tracked file’s discarded edits are usually replaced with older contents in place; the removed version is not necessarily a deleted file for the operating system to catch.

What We Have Today

The current VS Code documentation makes the distinction explicit. Discarding a tracked file restores its staged version, or the committed version if nothing is staged. Discarding an untracked file removes it. Untracked files can go to the Recycle Bin or Trash when git.discardUntrackedChangesToTrash is enabled and the environment supports it, but that is not guaranteed. The docs suggest checking Timeline local history or the system Trash after a mistake, while warning that neither is a guaranteed backup. The 2017 report should therefore not be read as a description of every current VS Code setup.

For a command-line workflow, I would first inspect the actual boundary:

These commands show different things: working-tree status, unstaged changes, staged changes, and the untracked paths a clean operation would remove. None of them saves the work. When I need to set aside a whole working state, git stash push -u can record tracked changes and untracked files before cleaning the tree. The -u flag does not include ignored files; -a does, with a much broader effect. A stash is useful, but it is an explicit temporary snapshot, not an automatic undo button for every discard.

The simpler long-term habit is still to commit work in small increments. Yet “remember to commit” cannot be the entire design answer. We use discard precisely when we are exploring, reorganizing, or uncertain whether something deserves a commit. Those are the moments when a reversible operation is most valuable.

Git is very good at remembering what we deliberately put into its history. A trash can would remember what we were about to throw away. The difference is small in the interface and enormous when we need to undo one click.

entry.title: RoPE: Properties, Patterns, and Long-Context Behavior
entry.content:
Rotary Position Embedding, usually called RoPE, is one of the most common positional encoding methods in modern decoder-only language models. It appears in models such as LLaMA and many of its descendants, and it is also the positional encoding used in CS336 Assignment 1.

RoPE is often introduced with one sentence: rotate the query and key vectors according to their positions. That description is correct, but it hides the most interesting part. The important question is not merely how to implement a rotation matrix. It is why rotating queries and keys makes the attention score depend on relative position, what mathematical invariants this creates, and why the same mechanism eventually becomes difficult to extrapolate to very long contexts.

The main idea of this post is:

We will derive this result and then study the main properties and patterns of RoPE:

  • rotations preserve vector norms;
  • rotations compose according to position addition;
  • attention scores depend on relative displacement;
  • different dimensions operate at different frequencies;
  • the resulting position kernel is oscillatory rather than strictly monotonic;
  • high-frequency dimensions create short-period behavior and possible aliasing;
  • rotating only $Q$ and $K$ is deliberate;
  • partial or half RoPE trades positional coverage for unrotated content dimensions;
  • long-context extensions are fundamentally frequency-scaling methods.

1. Why Does Attention Need Position Information?

Self-attention compares token representations through dot products. Without any positional signal, the mechanism has no direct notion of order. The sequence

and a reordered version contain the same token vectors, even though their meaning is different.

A causal mask helps, but it solves a different problem. It tells position $i$ that it may attend only to positions $j\leq i$. It does not explicitly tell the model how far away position $j$ is, nor does it create a continuous representation of relative distance.

This distinction is important:

  • causal masking controls visibility;
  • positional encoding represents location or distance.

RoPE is a way to inject position into the attention computation without adding a separate positional vector to the hidden state.

2. The Basic Two-Dimensional Rotation

Start with a two-dimensional vector $x=(x_1,x_2)^T$. Rotating it by angle $\phi$ gives:

Equivalently, if we identify $(x_1,x_2)$ with the complex number $z=x_1+ix_2$, the same operation is simply:

RoPE applies this operation to pairs of dimensions in a query or key vector. At sequence position $m$, the rotation angle is proportional to $m$:

where $\omega$ is a frequency assigned to that pair of dimensions.

The position does not produce an additive vector. It determines how far the content vector is rotated in its two-dimensional plane.

3. From One Rotation to the Full RoPE Matrix

Let the head dimension be $d$, where $d$ is even. Pair the coordinates:

The $k$-th pair receives its own frequency $\omega_k$. At position $m$, its angle is:

The full rotation is a block-diagonal matrix:

and the rotated vector is:

In the standard RoPE parameterization used by many LLMs, the frequencies are geometrically spaced:

or, depending on whether indexing starts at zero or one,

Here $\Theta$ is commonly set to $10{,}000$. The exact indexing convention varies between implementations, but the essential pattern is the same: the frequencies form a geometric progression from fast to slow.

The model does not learn these frequencies in standard RoPE. They are determined by the hyperparameter $\Theta$ and the head dimension.

4. The Central Derivation: Relative Position Appears in the Dot Product

Let $q_m$ be the content-dependent query at position $m$ and $k_n$ be the key at position $n$. RoPE produces:

The attention score is their dot product:

Using $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$:

For a rotation matrix, $Rm^T=R{-m}$. Rotations also compose additively:

Therefore:

and the score becomes:

This is the core property of RoPE. The query and key are individually transformed using absolute positions $m$ and $n$, but their interaction depends on the relative displacement $n-m$.

The content vectors $q_m$ and $k_n$ still matter. RoPE does not replace content similarity with distance-only attention. Instead, it gives the content interaction a position-dependent transformation.

The block-diagonal version

Because the full RoPE matrix is block diagonal, the same derivation applies independently to every two-dimensional frequency plane:

The final attention score is a sum of relative-position interactions evaluated at multiple frequencies.

5. Important Algebraic Properties

5.1 Norm preservation

Every rotation matrix is orthogonal:

Therefore:

RoPE changes direction but not magnitude.

This is useful for optimization. The positional transformation itself cannot amplify or shrink a vector. It only changes its phase in each two-dimensional plane. Of course, the overall Transformer can still change the norm through linear layers, RMSNorm, residual connections, and nonlinearities; norm preservation applies specifically to the rotation.

5.2 Composition by position addition

Rotating first by $a$ and then by $b$ is equivalent to rotating once by $a+b$:

This makes position shifts easy to reason about. If every position is shifted by the same offset $c$:

then their relative interaction is still governed by:

The shared offset cancels. This translation structure is one reason RoPE is naturally compatible with relative positions.

5.3 The origin is not special to the score

Because a common shift cancels inside $R_m^TR_n$, the attention score does not fundamentally depend on where the sequence starts. It depends on the distance between the two positions, together with their content vectors.

This does not mean that an entire Transformer becomes perfectly translation-invariant. Causal boundaries, finite context windows, padding, document delimiters, and the learned content representations can all break simple global invariance. The statement is specifically about the positional part of the $Q^TK$ interaction.

5.4 Relative position is not the same as distance

RoPE encodes the signed displacement $n-m$, not only the absolute distance $|n-m|$.

In general:

because the two matrices rotate in opposite directions. Therefore, the mechanism can distinguish “the key is 10 positions to the right” from “the key is 10 positions to the left,” subject to the causal mask and the content learned by the model.

6. Why Are There Many Frequencies?

If every pair of dimensions used the same frequency, all pairs would repeat with the same period. The model would have only one positional clock.

RoPE instead uses a geometric frequency schedule:

The corresponding period of one frequency is:

This produces a collection of clocks:

  • high-frequency pairs rotate quickly and detect fine local offsets;
  • low-frequency pairs rotate slowly and represent broader positional relationships.

The model can combine these signals to distinguish both nearby and distant positions.

A multi-scale analogy

The frequency spectrum is similar to using several measurement rulers:

  • a short ruler gives precise local resolution but wraps around quickly;
  • a long ruler covers a larger range but is less sensitive to small differences.

RoPE gives the attention mechanism many such rulers at once. A particular relative distance is represented by the vector of phases across all frequency pairs.

7. The Position Kernel: Oscillation and Decay

Consider a simplified setting where the content vectors are fixed and focus only on the positional contribution. In one two-dimensional plane, the relative-position term contains sine and cosine:

As $\Delta=n-m$ changes, this term oscillates. Across all frequency planes, the total positional interaction is a sum of oscillations:

The exact expression depends on the query and key components, but this simplified kernel is useful for understanding the pattern.

The original RoPE analysis highlights a decaying tendency of relative-position dependence as the distance increases. More precisely, the aggregate kernel often has a strong central peak and decreasing average correlation at larger distances, but it is not strictly monotonic. Because it is a sum of periodic functions, it can oscillate and produce secondary peaks.

This distinction matters:

  • “decaying on average” is a useful inductive bias;
  • “strictly decreases for every distance” is not a property of standard RoPE.

RoPE therefore favors nearby interactions without imposing a hard local window. The model can still attend to distant positions when the content-dependent query-key interaction makes them useful.

8. Periodicity, Phase Wrapping, and Aliasing

Every frequency is periodic:

For a single frequency $\omega_k$, positions separated by its period $T_k$ have the same phase:

This is phase wrapping. A high-frequency component wraps quickly; a low-frequency component wraps slowly.

The full vector of frequencies makes the combined representation much less ambiguous than any single frequency. However, at sufficiently long distances, multiple frequency components can become difficult to distinguish, especially when the model is evaluated far beyond the position range seen during training.

This is the connection between RoPE and aliasing. The model does not receive an unbounded, perfectly unique coordinate. It receives a collection of periodic phases.

Why high frequencies are fragile at long context

For a fixed frequency, the phase difference is:

As $\Delta$ grows, high-frequency components move through many cycles. Small changes in position can cause large phase changes, while large changes can land on similar phases after wrapping.

Low-frequency components are smoother and more stable over long distances, but they provide less local resolution. Long-context methods therefore often modify the frequency allocation or rescale the position index to make the learned phase range usable at a larger context length.

9. Why Rotate $Q$ and $K$, but Not $V$?

Attention has two conceptually different stages:

  1. compute how much each key should contribute;
  2. use those weights to aggregate the values.

RoPE is applied to $Q$ and $K$ because position should affect the matching score:

The value vector carries the content that will be transmitted after the matching decision. Keeping $V$ unrotated means the message itself is not transformed into a position-dependent coordinate system.

In standard RoPE:

This separation is not mathematically inevitable; it is an architectural choice. The key property of standard RoPE is that relative position enters the attention logits through $Q^TK$, while the value path remains position-agnostic.

10. Why Not Rotate the Input Hidden State $X$?

A natural question is: if position should affect the representation, why not rotate $X$ first and then compute $Q=XW_Q$ and $K=XW_K$?

Suppose we rotate the input:

Then the query becomes:

This is not generally the same as:

because the learned projection $W_Q$ does not generally commute with the rotation matrix:

The clean relative-position derivation depends on rotating the projected $Q$ and $K$ vectors:

not on rotating the input before arbitrary learned projections.

Rotating $X$ would entangle position with the input representation before the model decides how to form queries, keys, and values. RoPE instead injects position at the exact point where relative position is used: the attention matching operation.

11. Partial RoPE and Half RoPE

Standard RoPE rotates all dimensions of a head. Partial RoPE, also called half RoPE in some implementations, applies rotation only to a subset of the head dimension.

Let the head dimension be $d$ and let the rotary dimension be $d_r\leq d$. We split:

and apply:

The rotated part carries the relative-position mechanism. The pass-through part is not rotated and can preserve content features without phase modulation.

Why might this help? Full RoPE forces every query and key dimension to participate in the periodic positional transformation. Partial RoPE gives the model a mixture of:

  • position-aware dimensions;
  • position-neutral content dimensions.

This can be useful when the model benefits from reserving some dimensions for content matching that is less affected by position. The tradeoff is that the positional signal has lower dimensional capacity.

Partial RoPE is not the same as applying a smaller RoPE to every vector by truncating the model. The unrotated dimensions remain part of the attention dot product and still contribute content similarity.

12. RoPE and Inference with a KV Cache

RoPE is especially important during autoregressive inference because keys are usually cached.

Suppose a prompt occupies positions $0$ through $T-1$, and the next generated token is at position $T$. The new query must be rotated with position $T$:

Each cached key must retain the rotation corresponding to the position where it was originally created:

The score is then:

The important implementation consequence is that a cached key should not be re-rotated using the current decoding position. Its position is part of its identity.

This creates a common source of bugs: the position index used during decoding must continue from the prompt length, rather than restarting at zero for every generated token or every chunk.

RoPE itself does not require a KV cache, but the cache makes its position convention operationally important. In long-running generation, a position offset error changes every subsequent attention score.

13. Implementation Intuition

The full $d\times d$ rotation matrix is almost never materialized. Instead, implementations cache the cosine and sine values for every position and every rotary dimension.

For a vector split into two halves $x_1$ and $x_2$, one common representation is:

Then:

The exact pairing convention varies. Some implementations interleave the pairs as $(x_1,x_2),(x_3,x_4),\ldots$; others split the vector into two halves and pair the corresponding coordinates. Both can be correct, but the cosine/sine layout must match the chosen rotation convention.

The essential implementation invariants are:

  • head_dim or rotary_dim must be even;
  • the cosine and sine tensors must broadcast over batch and head dimensions;
  • the same position index must be used for the corresponding query and key;
  • RoPE must be applied independently to each attention head;
  • the cached cosine and sine values should use the correct device and dtype;
  • if only part of the head is rotary, the remaining dimensions must pass through unchanged.

RoPE has no learnable parameters in its standard form. The model learns how to use the rotated representations, but the rotation frequencies themselves are fixed by the configuration.

14. Long-Context Extrapolation

RoPE is often trained with a maximum context length $L{train}$ and later evaluated at a longer length $L{test}$. If $L{test}\gg L{train}$, several problems can appear.

14.1 Distribution shift in phase

During training, the model sees angles in the range:

At a longer context, it sees a phase range that may be far outside training. The model may not know how to interpret those unseen phase combinations.

14.2 High-frequency phase instability

High-frequency dimensions rotate many times over a long context. Their phases change rapidly and wrap around frequently. Low-frequency dimensions extrapolate more smoothly but may not resolve nearby positions as precisely.

14.3 Interpolation versus extrapolation

A long-context extension often tries to rescale the position indices or alter the frequency schedule so that the new positions remain within a phase range that resembles training.

The broad strategies include:

  • position interpolation: compress longer positions into the original trained range;
  • NTK-aware scaling: modify the frequency allocation so important frequencies cover the new context;
  • YaRN and related methods: combine frequency scaling with additional corrections and training choices;
  • other variants such as xPos: modify the rotary mechanism to improve stability over long distances.

The common principle is not “make the context length larger for free.” It is “change how positions map to phases so the model sees a more manageable distribution.” Long-context capability depends on both the position encoding and the training distribution.

15. RoPE Compared with Other Position Encodings

Learned absolute embeddings

A learned absolute embedding adds a vector $p_m$ to the token representation:

This is simple and expressive within the trained position range, but the model must store a representation for each position, and extrapolation beyond the learned table is difficult.

Sinusoidal absolute embeddings

The original Transformer uses fixed sine and cosine vectors. They can represent positions without learned parameters and have useful algebraic structure, but the positional signal is added to the hidden representation rather than inserted directly into the $QK$ matching operation.

ALiBi

ALiBi adds a distance-dependent linear bias to attention logits:

for head-specific slope $b_h$. It directly biases attention toward nearby positions and has a different extrapolation behavior from RoPE.

RoPE

RoPE multiplies $Q$ and $K$ by position-dependent rotations. Its distinctive properties are:

  • no learned positional parameters in standard form;
  • norm preservation;
  • a clean relative-position derivation through $R_m^TR_n$;
  • multiple geometric frequencies;
  • periodic phase behavior that must be considered for long contexts.

There is no universally best positional encoding. The right choice depends on the model architecture, training context, inference length, and desired inductive bias.

16. A Compact Summary of RoPE’s Properties

PropertyMathematical reasonPractical implication
Norm preserving$R_m^TR_m=I$Position changes direction, not magnitude
Relative interaction$Rm^TR_n=R{n-m}$Attention can depend on relative displacement
Translation structure$R{m+c}^TR{n+c}=R_m^TR_n$A shared position offset cancels in the score
Multi-scale resolutionGeometric frequencies $\omega_k$Fast and slow positional clocks coexist
Periodicity$R(\phi+2\pi)=R(\phi)$Phase wrapping and aliasing can occur
Content preservation in $V$RoPE is applied to $Q,K$ onlyPosition changes matching, not the transmitted value
Parameter-free standard formFrequencies are fixedNo positional weights are learned
Partial RoPERotate only $d_r<d$ dimensionsMix position-aware and pass-through features

17. Common Mistakes

Confusing RoPE with the causal mask

RoPE does not prevent access to future tokens. The causal mask does that. RoPE provides a position-dependent transformation; the mask controls visibility.

Applying RoPE to $V$ by default

Standard RoPE rotates $Q$ and $K$, not $V$. Rotating $V$ changes the value path and is a different architectural choice.

Rotating the hidden state before projection

The clean relative-position derivation applies to $R_mW_Qx_m$ and $R_nW_Kx_n$. In general, $W_QR_m\neq R_mW_Q$, so rotating $X$ before the learned projections is not equivalent.

Using the wrong position offset in generation

When decoding after a prompt, the next token starts at the prompt length. Restarting positions from zero can silently corrupt every subsequent attention score.

Mixing pairing conventions

Interleaved pairs and half-split pairs are both possible. The error comes from using one convention for $x$ and another for the cached sine/cosine layout.

Assuming the positional kernel is strictly monotonic

RoPE uses a sum of periodic functions. Its average dependence may decay with relative distance, but the exact score can oscillate and have secondary peaks.

Treating long-context extension as only a memory problem

Even if the hardware can store a longer context, the model may not know how to interpret the new phase distribution. Context extension is also a positional-distribution and training problem.

Conclusion

RoPE is elegant because a simple local operation creates a useful global property. Rotate the query at position $m$ and the key at position $n$:

Then their attention interaction becomes:

Absolute positions disappear from the positional part of the interaction, leaving relative displacement.

The rest of RoPE follows from this algebra: rotations preserve norms, compose additively, create a multi-scale frequency spectrum, and introduce periodic phase behavior. Those same properties explain both its strengths and its limitations. RoPE gives Transformers a clean relative-position inductive bias, but long-context inference must account for frequency resolution, phase wrapping, aliasing, and position-index consistency.

For LLM systems, RoPE is therefore more than a small positional-encoding layer. It is part of the contract between the model architecture and the inference runtime: the query, cached keys, sequence offsets, rotary dimension, and frequency schedule must all agree.

References

  1. Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding, 2021.
  2. Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, 2017.
  3. Stanford CS336, Assignment 1: Building a Transformer LM.
